Aim and objectives

Aim. To read and appraise forest plots and pooled results from meta-analyses with confidence.

At the end of this workbook, you should be able to:

  1. Interpret a forest plot: individual studies, weights, confidence intervals, the pooled diamond and the line of no effect.
  2. Explain how heterogeneity is explored using subgroup and sensitivity analyses.
  3. Interpret pooled time-to-event curves and hazard ratios from a meta-analysis.
  4. Explain how intention-to-treat analysis and missing data affect pooled estimates.
  5. Complete all 30 worked challenges, scoring at least 24 (80%), before you open the working.
  6. Turn all 50 flashcards and mark at least 40 as 'Got it' by the end of today's session.

Part 1 · Core ideas

Category 113.13 · Systematic reviews and meta-analysis

13.4.7Reading and appraising forest plots

Big idea. A forest plot is a table drawn as a picture: each row is a study, each square its estimate, each line its uncertainty, and the diamond the answer the review gives.
Picture it as a row of archers, each with an arrow and a spread of misses, and the team average marked as a diamond.

Syllabus: Critically appraise systematic review and meta-analysis

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 47 · Forest plots and line of no effect →

The story in plain words. Read a forest plot like a row of forecasts with error bars. Each study gets a row. The square marks its point estimate, and its area shows the weight the study carries, so big precise studies have big squares. The horizontal line is the 95% confidence interval: a long line means an imprecise study, and an arrowhead means it runs off the scale. The vertical line of no effect sits at 1 for ratios and 0 for differences. A study whose line crosses it is not statistically significant on its own. The diamond is the pooled estimate: its centre is the summary result and its width the confidence interval. ((? In the diagram, which study carries most weight and why? ?)) Study D, with 50%, because it has the most participants and events and so the smallest variance. Here the pooled risk ratio is 0.69 (0.55 to 0.86): no small study convinces alone, yet together they show a clear benefit. That is the point of pooling.

Anatomy of a forest plot: five trials, fixed-effect pooled risk ratio, numbered features. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. Lewis and Clarke traced the history of the forest plot in the BMJ in 2001, explaining that it lets readers see both the wood (the overall result) and the trees (each study). Its nickname, the blobbogram, comes from the squares. When outcomes are continuous and measured on different scales, the axis shows a standardised mean difference. Jacob Cohen suggested reading 0.2 as small, 0.5 as medium and 0.8 as large.

From everyday life to the clinic. Appraising a forest plot means asking which side favours treatment (read the axis labels, never assume), how many studies sit on each side, whether the intervals overlap, and whether subgroup diamonds differ. The pooled diamond is almost always the most precise estimate on the page, because it combines everyone. Then appraise the review behind it: a clear question, a comprehensive search, quality assessment of each study, sensible pooling, and an honest account of heterogeneity and publication bias.

A forest plot is a row of archers: each square is one archer's average, its size how many arrows they shot, its line the spread, and the diamond the weighted team average. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Classic traps: confusing square size (weight) with line length (precision); reading a point estimate on the wrong side when the axis labels are reversed; calling a study significant when its line crosses the null. The confidence interval is drawn horizontally; the only vertical line is the line of no effect. An effect size on a standardised axis is a standardised mean difference, not a raw score difference.

The four forest plot features examiners swap: square size, line length, the vertical line of no effect, and what crossing it means. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Mantel N, Haenszel W (1959). Statistical aspects of the analysis of data from retrospective studies of disease. Journal of the National Cancer Institute, 22: 719-748.
  2. Deeks JJ (2002). Issues in the selection of a summary statistic for meta-analysis of clinical trials with binary outcomes. Statistics in Medicine, 21: 1575-1600.
  3. Higgins JPT, Thomas J, Chandler J, et al. (eds) (2023). Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6.4. Cochrane.
  4. Higgins JPT, Thompson SG (2002). Quantifying heterogeneity in a meta-analysis. Statistics in Medicine, 21: 1539-1558.

13.9.6.4Reading pooled time-to-event curves

Big idea. A survival curve and a cumulative incidence curve are mirror images of the same data: one counts who is still event-free, the other who has had the event.
Picture it as a glass emptying into a jug from the same pour.

Syllabus: Interpret survival curves

Read more in your textbookStatistics, page 98 · Survival analysis: Kaplan-Meier →Evidence-Based Medicine, page 120 · Appraising prognosis studies →

The story in plain words. Pour water from a glass into a jug and you can describe the same moment two ways: how much is left in the glass, or how much has reached the jug. A Kaplan-Meier survival curve shows the proportion still event-free, stepping down at each event. Plotted as cumulative incidence, 1 - S(t), the same data step up. The horizontal axis is time from each person's entry, not calendar time. Small vertical ticks mark censoring: people who left follow-up without the event. Each step is calculated among those still at risk, shown in the row beneath the axis. The median survival time is where the curve crosses 50%. ((? In the diagram, what is the median time to the event? ?)) 18 months, where survival first falls to or below 50% and the incidence curve rises past it. If a curve never reaches 50% within follow-up, the median cannot be determined.

One Kaplan-Meier analysis drawn both ways, with censoring ticks, numbers at risk and the median. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. Edward Kaplan and Paul Meier published the product-limit estimator in 1958. It solved the problem of people who drop out before the event: they contribute information for as long as they are observed. Bland and Altman's 1998 BMJ note explains how to read these probabilities and why the right-hand tail of a curve, where few remain at risk, is the least reliable part.

From everyday life to the clinic. Meta-analyses can pool time-to-event data from several cohorts, for example conversion from depression to bipolar disorder in young people. The figure then shows one curve per study plus a pooled curve. The spread between study curves at a chosen time hints at heterogeneity. Ask four questions: what is the event, what is time zero, how many remain at risk at the end, and does the pooled curve ever reach 50%?

Kaplan-Meier survival S(t) is what is left in the glass; cumulative incidence 1 minus S(t) is what has reached the jug. Levels use the Kaplan-Meier estimates from the lesson's cohort. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Traps: refusing to call a rising curve Kaplan-Meier; reading the vertical axis as people surviving when it shows cumulative incidence; reporting a median from a curve that never reaches 50%. Study type is the other trap: pooled curves from several cohorts come from a meta-analysis, not from a single cohort study.

If fewer than half the participants have the event during follow-up, the median time to event cannot be read from the curve. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. L'Abbé KA, Detsky AS, O'Rourke K (1987). Meta-analysis in clinical research. Annals of Internal Medicine, 107: 224-233.
  2. Cochran WG (1954). The combination of estimates from different experiments. Biometrics, 10: 101-129.
  3. Higgins JPT, Thompson SG (2002). Quantifying heterogeneity in a meta-analysis. Statistics in Medicine, 21: 1539-1558.

Category 213.8 · Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis

3.2.22Intention to treat and missing data

Big idea. Randomisation is the only thing that makes two groups comparable, and every decision about who to analyse is a decision about how much of that protection to keep.
Picture it as once randomised, always analysed.

Syllabus: Intention to treat, per protocol, missing data methods and sensitivity analysis

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 98 · Intention-to-treat and missing data →

The story in plain words. Intention to treat analyses everyone in the group they were randomised to, whatever happened afterwards. Patients who stopped the drug, never started it or took the other one all stay where randomisation put them. It is not a technicality. Randomisation is what balanced the groups on everything, measured and unmeasured, and any departure from it unbalances them again. ITT also mirrors real prescribing, because real patients stop drugs. Per protocol analyses only those who completed treatment as planned, and is vulnerable to bias precisely because completing is not random. ((? Why is ITT described as conservative? ?)) It biases towards the null, so a superiority trial that is positive under ITT has earned it. In a non-inferiority trial that same bias favours the new drug, which is why both analyses must be shown.

Once randomised, always analysed: intention to treat keeps every patient in the arm they were allocated to, preserving the balance that randomisation created

The people and the evidence. Missing data has to be handled somehow. Complete-case analysis drops anyone with a gap, losing power and possibly introducing bias. Last observation carried forward lets the last score stand for all later ones, which is simple and assumes nothing changed after drop-out. Lachin (2016) showed it is not reliably conservative, despite being described that way for years. Multiple imputation creates several plausible completed datasets, analyses each and pools the results, so the uncertainty is carried through. It is valid when data are missing at random. Mixed models use all the observed data without imputing anything.

From everyday life to the clinic. Best case and worst case analyses fill in the most and least favourable outcomes for the missing, which brackets the possible truth rather than estimating it. A sensitivity analysis repeats the whole analysis under different assumptions and asks whether the conclusion survives. If the worst-case analysis still favours treatment, the result is robust. It is not the same as a subgroup analysis, which asks whether the effect differs between kinds of patient.

Intention to treat compares all 50 gym people with all 50 others, drop-outs and crossovers included: that is what offering a gym membership achieves in real life, and it keeps the two groups as alike as randomisation made them

Where the exam tries to catch you. The first trap is a stem describing a per-protocol analysis and calling it intention to treat. Look for whether drop-outs were kept. The second is the claim that LOCF is conservative. The third is confusing sensitivity analysis with subgroup analysis: one tests the assumptions, the other tests the patients.

Sources
  1. Gardner MJ, Altman DG (1986). Confidence intervals rather than P values: estimation rather than hypothesis testing. BMJ, 292: 746-750.
  2. Glass GV (1976). Primary, secondary, and meta-analysis of research. Educational Researcher, 5(10): 3-8.
  3. Hollis S, Campbell F (1999). What is meant by intention to treat analysis? BMJ, 319: 670-674.
  4. Hollis S, Campbell F (1999). What is meant by intention to treat analysis? Survey of published randomised controlled trials. BMJ, 319: 670-674.
  5. Kirkwood BR, Sterne JAC (2003). Essential Medical Statistics, 2nd ed. Blackwell.

3.2.23Meta-analysis: purpose and models

Big idea. A meta-analysis adds the power of many small studies together, and adds their biases together at the same time.
Picture it as pooling several small surveys.

Syllabus: The purpose and limits of meta-analysis, fixed and random effects, reading a forest plot

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 41 · Systematic reviews and meta-analysis →

The story in plain words. A meta-analysis pools the results of several studies into one estimate with greater power and precision. It lets small but real effects be detected and lets consistency across studies be examined. What it cannot do is remove bias in the studies it pools. Garbage in, garbage out. The particular danger is publication bias: small negative studies are less likely to be published, so the pooled effect is inflated by what was never there to pool. Trial registries and funnel plots are the defences. Reading a forest plot is mechanical. Each study is a square whose size is its weight, with a horizontal line for its confidence interval. The vertical line is no effect, 1 for ratios and 0 for differences. The diamond at the foot is the pooled estimate and its width is its confidence interval.

Reading a forest plot: the bigger the square the more weight, the wider the line the less precision, the diamond is the pooled estimate, and anything crossing the null line is not significant on its own

The people and the evidence. Borenstein and colleagues (2010) set out the two models. A fixed effect model assumes there is one true effect and that differences between studies are chance. It weights by precision and gives a narrower confidence interval. A random effects model assumes a distribution of true effects, adds between-study variance, usually written tau squared, and gives a wider interval. Small studies get relatively more weight under random effects than under fixed.

From everyday life to the clinic. Use fixed effects when heterogeneity is low and random effects when the studies differ in populations or methods. The crucial caveat is that random effects does not fix heterogeneity, it only acknowledges it, and a pooled estimate from wildly different trials is a wrong answer given politely. ((? The diamond touches the vertical line. What follows? ?)) The pooled result is not statistically significant. And intervals that barely overlap are the visual sign of heterogeneity, before any test is run.

Pooling reviews: the restaurant with a thousand reviews should weigh far more than the one with three. A meta-analysis weights each study by its precision in exactly this way; the diamond is the weighted average

Where the exam tries to catch you. The first trap is the claim that meta-analysis corrects for bias in the original studies. It cannot. The second is square size, which represents weight and not effect size. The third is the assumption that random effects is always the safer choice; it widens the interval and shifts weight towards small studies, which are the ones most likely to be biased.

Sources
  1. Egger M, Davey Smith G, Schneider M, Minder C (1997). Bias in meta-analysis detected by a simple graphical test. BMJ, 315: 629-634.
  2. Borenstein M et al. (2010). A basic introduction to fixed-effect and random-effects models. Res Synth Methods, 1: 97-111.
  3. Egger M et al. (1997). Bias in meta-analysis detected by a simple, graphical test. BMJ, 315: 629-634.
  4. Higgins JPT et al. (2003). Measuring inconsistency in meta-analyses. BMJ, 327: 557-560.

3.2.25Heterogeneity and sensitivity analysis

Big idea. Before trusting a pooled number you have to ask whether the studies were answering the same question, and heterogeneity is the measure of how far they were not.
Picture it as averaging apples with pears.

Syllabus: Detecting and responding to heterogeneity, funnel plots and related methods

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 55 · Heterogeneity, I² and fixed vs random effects →Economic Evaluation, QI & Governance, page 33 · Sensitivity analysis and tornado diagrams →

The story in plain words. Heterogeneity is variation between studies beyond what chance explains. The first detection is visual: confidence intervals on the forest plot that barely overlap. Cochran's Q tests it formally, but it has low power, which is why a threshold of p below 0.10 is used rather than the usual 0.05. I squared is the more useful figure: the percentage of total variation due to heterogeneity rather than chance, with 25% low, 50% moderate and 75% high. Because it is a percentage it compares across meta-analyses. The Galbraith or radial plot puts the z score against precision; points falling outside a band of about 2 units are the outlying studies.

The funnel plot: large studies cluster at the top near the pooled estimate; small studies scatter widely at the bottom. The empty lower right tells you which small studies were never published

The people and the evidence. Egger and colleagues (1997) gave us the test for funnel plot asymmetry. A funnel plot puts effect size against precision. With no publication bias the scatter is a symmetrical inverted funnel, wide at the bottom where small imprecise studies sit. An empty lower corner means small studies with unexciting results are missing. Egger's test quantifies the asymmetry, and trim and fill adjusts the pooled estimate for it. The L'Abbe plot does something different, putting the event rate in the treatment arm against the control arm for each trial.

From everyday life to the clinic. There are four honest responses to heterogeneity. Look for a clinical or methodological explanation, through subgroup analysis or meta-regression. Switch to a random effects model. Run a sensitivity analysis. Or decide not to pool at all, which is sometimes the only defensible answer. A sensitivity analysis here means excluding low-quality studies, or the largest study, or the outliers, or changing the model, and seeing whether the pooled estimate holds. ((? What does it mean if dropping the largest trial reverses the conclusion? ?)) That the conclusion was that trial's, not the literature's.

Eight studies as eight darts: when they cluster, one pooled number is honest; when they scatter widely, ask why before pooling (different patients, doses, outcomes) and use a random-effects model

Where the exam tries to catch you. The first trap is the p value threshold for Cochran's Q, which is 0.10 and not 0.05, because the test is underpowered. The second is an I squared of 75% offered as acceptable. The third is the belief that switching to random effects has dealt with heterogeneity. It has acknowledged it and widened the interval; the apples and the pears are still in the same bowl.

Sources
  1. Galbraith RF (1988). A note on graphical presentation of estimated odds ratios from several clinical trials. Stat Med, 7: 889-894.
  2. Egger M, Davey Smith G, Phillips AN (1997). Meta-analysis: principles and procedures. BMJ, 315: 1533-1537.
  3. Kirkwood BR, Sterne JAC (2003). Essential Medical Statistics, 2nd ed. Blackwell.

Part 2 · Worked challenges

Try each one first. Then show the working and read the rule.

Challenge 1 · 13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.7
Executive function in adults with ADHD versus healthy controls, grouped by type of task. Negative values mean poorer performance in ADHD; teal line = no difference; heterogeneity is shown under each subtotal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Which statistic was most likely used to produce each study's estimate in the figure?
  1. Pearson's r
  2. Cohen's kappa
  3. Student's t
  4. Cohen's d (Hedges' g)
  5. Spearman's rho
Show the working
Answer: D Cohen's d (Hedges' g)

The 'effect size' on this forest plot is a standardised mean difference: the difference in group means divided by the pooled standard deviation, so it has no units and 0 means no difference. That is Cohen's d, or Hedges' g with a small-sample correction.

Pearson's r and Spearman's rho are correlations, a t statistic tests a difference rather than describing its size, and Cohen's kappa measures agreement between raters.

Rule: SMD axis = Cohen's d family.
Trap: Confusing Cohen's d with Cohen's kappa.
Cohen's d (or Hedges' g) is the difference in means divided by the pooled standard deviation: here the ADHD group sits half an SD lower. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Cohen J (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, 2nd ed. Lawrence Erlbaum.

Challenge 2 · 13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.7
Executive function in adults with ADHD versus healthy controls, grouped by type of task. Negative values mean poorer performance in ADHD; teal line = no difference; heterogeneity is shown under each subtotal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In the figure, the term 'effect size' on the horizontal axis corresponds to which quantity?
  1. Standardised mean difference
  2. Inverse of the variance
  3. Inverse of the sample size
  4. Logarithm of the standard error
  5. Correlation multiplied by sample size
Show the working
Answer: A Standardised mean difference

'Effect size' on a continuous forest plot means the standardised mean difference: how far apart the group means are, in standard deviation units.

Inverse variance gives each study's weight, and the standard error and sample size describe precision. None of those is the size of the effect.

Rule: Effect size on a continuous forest plot = SMD.
Trap: Mixing up the effect with the weight.
On a continuous forest plot the 'effect size' axis is the standardised mean difference: the gap between group means in SD units. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Cohen J (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, 2nd ed. Lawrence Erlbaum.

Challenge 3 · 13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.7
Relapse at 12 months: a group, individual or digital relapse-prevention programme versus usual care in recurrent depression. Squares sized by inverse-variance weight; gold diamonds are subgroup estimates, the burgundy diamond the overall estimate (inverse-variance fixed effect); teal line = no effect; heterogeneity is shown under each subtotal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
What is the type of graph shown in the figure?
  1. Funnel plot
  2. Forest plot (blobbogram)
  3. Galbraith plot
  4. L'Abbé plot
  5. Scatter plot
Show the working
Answer: B Forest plot (blobbogram)

Individual study estimates with horizontal confidence lines, a vertical line of no effect and a pooled diamond define a forest plot, nicknamed the blobbogram.

A funnel plot is a scatter of effect against precision, a Galbraith plot shows standardised effect against precision, and a L'Abbé plot shows treatment against control event rates.

Rule: Squares + lines + diamond = forest plot.
Trap: Calling it a funnel plot because it summarises several studies.
Four meta-analysis graphs side by side: only the forest plot has study rows with confidence lines and a pooled diamond. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Lewis S, Clarke M (2001). Forest plots: trying to see the wood and the trees. BMJ, 322: 1479-1480.

Challenge 4 · 13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.7
Relapse at 12 months: a group, individual or digital relapse-prevention programme versus usual care in recurrent depression. gold diamonds are subgroup estimates, the burgundy diamond the overall estimate (inverse-variance fixed effect); teal line = no effect; heterogeneity is shown under each subtotal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In the figure, which feature shows how much weight each study carries in the pooled estimate?
  1. The length of the horizontal line
  2. The order in which studies are listed
  3. The distance of the square from the line of no effect
  4. The size of the square for each study
  5. Weight cannot be seen on a forest plot
Show the working
Answer: D The size of the square for each study

The area of each square is drawn in proportion to the study's weight in the pooled estimate, which is also printed in the weight column.

Line length shows the confidence interval (precision) and the square's distance from the line of no effect shows the size of the effect. Large, precise studies usually have big squares on short lines.

Rule: Square size = weight. Line length = precision. Position = effect.
Trap: Reading line length as weight.
Square area shows weight; line length shows the confidence interval. Big squares usually sit on short lines. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Lewis S, Clarke M (2001). Forest plots: trying to see the wood and the trees. BMJ, 322: 1479-1480.

Challenge 5 · 13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.7
Relapse at 12 months: a group, individual or digital relapse-prevention programme versus usual care in recurrent depression. Squares sized by inverse-variance weight; gold diamonds are subgroup estimates, the burgundy diamond the overall estimate (inverse-variance fixed effect); teal line = no effect; heterogeneity is shown under each subtotal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In the figure, which study has a point estimate favouring usual care over the relapse-prevention programme?
  1. Study 5 (2018)
  2. Study 1 (2012)
  3. Study 2 (2014)
  4. Study 4 (2015)
  5. Study 6 (2020)
Show the working
Answer: A Study 5 (2018)

With relapse as the outcome, a risk ratio below 1 favours the programme and above 1 favours usual care. Study 5 has a point estimate of 1.35, to the right of 1.

Its interval, 0.70 to 2.60, crosses 1, so the result is not statistically significant. 'Favours' describes direction; significance comes from the interval.

Rule: Read the axis labels: which side favours which arm.
Trap: Confusing 'favours' with 'statistically significant'.
With relapse as the outcome, a point estimate right of 1 favours usual care; Study 5's interval still crosses 1, so it is not significant. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Lewis S, Clarke M (2001). Forest plots: trying to see the wood and the trees. BMJ, 322: 1479-1480.

Challenge 6 · 13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.7
Executive function in adults with ADHD versus healthy controls, grouped by type of task. Negative values mean poorer performance in ADHD; teal line = no difference; heterogeneity is shown under each subtotal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
According to the figure, what is the approximate magnitude of the pooled difference in executive function between adults with ADHD and controls?
  1. About 0.1 standard deviations
  2. About 1.0 standard deviation
  3. About 1.5 standard deviations
  4. It cannot be determined
  5. About 0.5 standard deviations
Show the working
Answer: E About 0.5 standard deviations

The overall standardised mean difference is -0.50: adults with ADHD score about half a standard deviation lower than controls.

Cohen's rough guide reads 0.2 as small, 0.5 as medium and 0.8 as large. The minus sign shows direction only, so the magnitude is about 0.5 SD.

Rule: Cohen's guide: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.
Trap: Treating the minus sign as part of the magnitude.
Cohen's rough guide reads 0.2 as small, 0.5 as medium and 0.8 as large; the sign only gives direction. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Cohen J (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, 2nd ed. Lawrence Erlbaum.

Challenge 7 · 13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.7
Executive function in adults with ADHD versus healthy controls, grouped by type of task. Negative values mean poorer performance in ADHD; teal line = no difference; heterogeneity is shown under each subtotal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In the figure, which study found better executive function in the ADHD group than in controls?
  1. Study A (2011)
  2. None of the studies
  3. Study D (2010)
  4. Study E (2015)
  5. Study F (2019)
Show the working
Answer: B None of the studies

Every study's point estimate lies to the left of zero, so every study found poorer executive function in the ADHD group.

Study D's interval (-0.68 to 0.08) crosses zero, so its result is compatible with no difference, but its best estimate still points the same way. No study found better function in ADHD.

Rule: Direction comes from the point estimate; significance from the interval.
Trap: Reading 'interval crosses zero' as 'favours the other group'.
Direction comes from the point estimate and significance from the interval: Study D points to poorer performance in ADHD, though not significantly. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Lewis S, Clarke M (2001). Forest plots: trying to see the wood and the trees. BMJ, 322: 1479-1480.

Challenge 8 · 13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.4.7
Executive function in adults with ADHD versus healthy controls, grouped by type of task. Negative values mean poorer performance in ADHD; teal line = no difference; heterogeneity is shown under each subtotal. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In the figure, which individual study gives the most precise estimate?
  1. Study A (2011)
  2. Study D (2010)
  3. Study E (2015)
  4. Study C (2017)
  5. Study F (2019)
Show the working
Answer: D Study C (2017)

The most precise single study has the narrowest confidence interval, which is the shortest horizontal line.

Study C runs from -0.72 to -0.38, a width of 0.34, narrower than any other study. It also carries the largest weight in the pooled estimate.

Rule: Shortest horizontal line = most precise single study.
Trap: Choosing the study with the largest effect.
The most precise single study has the shortest line: Study C, width 0.34, which also carries the most weight. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Lewis S, Clarke M (2001). Forest plots: trying to see the wood and the trees. BMJ, 322: 1479-1480.

Challenge 9 · 13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.9.6.4
Conversion to bipolar disorder in young people after a first depressive episode: five studies and a pooled curve, with numbers at risk; vertical ticks mark censored participants. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In the figure, what does the vertical axis represent?
  1. The proportion still free of bipolar disorder
  2. The proportion with bipolar disorder at study entry
  3. The cumulative proportion of young people who have converted to bipolar disorder
  4. The proportion who recovered from depression
  5. The follow-up time in each study
Show the working
Answer: C The cumulative proportion of young people who have converted to bipolar disorder

The curves start at 0% and rise, so the vertical axis is the cumulative proportion of young people who have converted to bipolar disorder.

A survival-style curve would start at 100% and fall. Always read both axis labels before interpreting a time-to-event graph; time is on the horizontal axis.

Rule: Rising curve from 0% = cumulative incidence of the event.
Trap: Reading the curve as survival.
A curve that starts at 0% and rises shows the cumulative proportion who have had the event, here conversion to bipolar disorder. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Bland JM, Altman DG (1998). Survival probabilities (the Kaplan-Meier method). BMJ, 317: 1572.

Challenge 10 · 13.13 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis · 13.9.6.4
Conversion to bipolar disorder in young people after a first depressive episode: five studies and a pooled curve, with numbers at risk; vertical ticks mark censored participants. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In the figure, what does the horizontal axis represent?
  1. Time from onset of bipolar disorder to treatment
  2. Time since each participant entered the cohort
  3. Time since first developing depressive symptoms
  4. Time taken to respond to an antidepressant
  5. Time from conversion to the end of the study
Show the working
Answer: B Time since each participant entered the cohort

In time-to-event analysis each participant's clock starts at time zero, usually entry into the study, whatever the calendar date of entry.

Follow-up then runs until the event (here, conversion) or censoring. Illness onset, treatment response and time after the event are not what the axis shows.

Rule: x-axis = time from a defined start (time zero).
Trap: Assuming time zero is illness onset.
In time-to-event analysis each person's clock starts at entry, so follow-up from different calendar dates is lined up at time zero. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Bland JM, Altman DG (1998). Survival probabilities (the Kaplan-Meier method). BMJ, 317: 1572.

Intention-to-treat preserves the balance created by randomisation and reflects what happens when a treatment is prescribed in practice, including non-adherence. It gives a conservative estimate of efficacy but an honest estimate of effectiveness.

Rule: ITT: analyse as randomised, regardless of what happened next.

Answer: B Last observation carried forward

LOCF is simple but assumes the patient would not have changed after dropping out. In a condition that improves with time it can flatter the treatment arm with the higher drop-out, and it understates variability. Mixed models and multiple imputation are now preferred.

Rule: LOCF: the last score stands in for all later missing scores.
Trap: Treating LOCF as conservative in every setting.
After week 6 the carried-forward line is flat at 14, so if the patient would have kept improving the method records too high a score at week 12 (illustrative).

Answer: C Sensitivity analysis

A result that survives several reasonable ways of handling missing data, outliers or model choices is robust. Sensitivity analyses are used in trials, meta-analyses and economic evaluations alike.

Rule: Sensitivity analysis = same question, different assumptions, does the answer hold?
Trap: Confusing with subgroup analysis.
The four analyses side by side: three intervals stay above zero, the worst-case interval reaches -1, so the conclusion holds under most but not all assumptions (illustrative).

Challenge 14 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.22
ArmAllocatedStopped earlyCompleted allocated treatmentResponded
New adjunctive drug18030 (nausea, moved to usual care)15095
Usual care180018090
Flow of 360 patients with bipolar depression through the trial
The table shows the flow of 360 patients with bipolar depression randomised equally to a new adjunctive drug or to usual care. Among the 180 on the new drug, 30 stop it early because of nausea and move to usual care; of the remaining 150, 95 respond. All 180 usual-care patients complete the trial and 90 respond. In the primary analysis, how should the 30 patients who stopped the new drug be handled?
  1. Analysed in the usual-care group, since that is the treatment they received
  2. Excluded from the analysis because they did not complete the allocated treatment
  3. Analysed in the new-drug group, as originally randomised
  4. Analysed only in a per-protocol completer analysis
  5. Given reduced weight in proportion to the time they spent on the drug
Show the working
Answer: C Analysed in the new-drug group, as originally randomised

Randomisation balances known and unknown confounders between arms only if the groups are analysed as allocated. Patients who stop a drug are not a random subset; they are often the ones with worse side effects or worse illness. Removing or moving them reintroduces exactly the selection bias that randomisation was meant to abolish. Intention to treat also answers the pragmatic question of what happens when you decide to offer the drug.

Here the 30 patients who stopped because of nausea must stay in the new-drug arm, so the intention-to-treat denominator is 180, not 150. Their response rate counts against the drug, which is appropriate because intolerance is part of real-world effectiveness. A per-protocol analysis of the 150 completers (95 / 150 = 63%) can be given alongside as a sensitivity analysis, but it will tend to flatter the drug compared with the intention-to-treat figure.

Distractors describe 'as treated' and 'completer' analyses; both are legitimate secondary analyses but neither is the primary analysis of an RCT.

Rule: Intention to treat: once randomised, always analysed in that arm.
Trap: Moving switchers to the comparator arm because that is what they actually took.
Intention to treat keeps all 180 in the drug arm, including the 30 who stopped: 95/180 = 53% versus 90/180 = 50%; dropping the 30 would give 95/150 = 63%

Source: Hollis S, Campbell F (1999). What is meant by intention to treat analysis? Survey of published randomised controlled trials. BMJ, 319: 670-674.

Challenge 15 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.22

Treatment completion in a 16-week trial of a new SNRI versus placebo in generalised anxiety disorder
A 16-week trial randomises 300 adults with generalised anxiety disorder to a new SNRI or placebo. The table shows how many patients in each arm had stopped their allocated treatment by the end. Which of the following statements about an intention to treat analysis of this trial is INCORRECT?
  1. It analyses every randomised patient in the arm to which they were allocated
  2. It includes the 65 patients who stopped their allocated treatment
  3. It analyses only those patients who completed the treatment they were allocated
  4. It preserves the balance of known and unknown prognostic factors created by randomisation
  5. It is generally preferred to a per protocol analysis for the primary analysis of a superiority trial
Show the working
Answer: C It analyses only those patients who completed the treatment they were allocated

Intention to treat analysis keeps every randomised participant in the group to which they were assigned, regardless of whether they took the treatment, switched or dropped out. Its purpose is to preserve the comparability that randomisation created and to estimate the effect of the policy of offering the treatment, as it would play out in practice. Removing people after randomisation reintroduces selection: those who stop a drug often differ in prognosis from those who continue.

In this trial 40 drug-arm and 25 placebo-arm patients stopped treatment. Under ITT all 150 in each arm are analysed as randomised, with sensible handling of missing outcomes (for example multiple imputation, with sensitivity analyses). Restricting the analysis to the 110 and 125 completers is a per protocol analysis; it may estimate the effect of actually taking the drug but is vulnerable to bias when drop-out differs between arms, as here.

The exam uses 'select the incorrect statement' and plants the per protocol definition among true ITT statements. Any option that says ITT analyses 'only those who received' or 'only completers' is the false one.

Rule: Intention to treat: analyse everyone as randomised, drop-outs included; per protocol: analyse only completers.
Trap: Mistaking the per protocol definition for intention to treat because it sounds like 'treating as intended'.
Intention to treat analyses all 150 in each arm, stopped or not; a per protocol analysis would keep only the 110 and 125 completers

Source: Hollis S, Campbell F (1999). What is meant by intention to treat analysis? Survey of published randomised controlled trials. BMJ, 319: 670-674.

Challenge 16 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.22

Probiotic supplement8017 (stopped or lost)63
Sertraline8011 (missed final assessment)69
Participant flow in a 12-week trial of a probiotic supplement versus sertraline
A 12-week trial randomised 160 outpatients with moderate depression to a probiotic supplement (n = 80) or sertraline (n = 80). By week 12, 17 participants in the probiotic arm had stopped the supplement or were lost to follow-up, and 11 in the sertraline arm had not attended their final assessment. The table shows the participant flow. Which denominators should be used when reporting the primary outcome of response at 12 weeks?
  1. 63 for the probiotic arm and 69 for sertraline
  2. 80 for the probiotic arm and 69 for sertraline
  3. 80 for the probiotic arm and 80 for sertraline
  4. 63 for the probiotic arm and 80 for sertraline
  5. The trial cannot be reported because of the differential drop-out
Show the working
Answer: C 80 for the probiotic arm and 80 for sertraline

Intention to treat means that the groups compared are exactly the groups created by randomisation. Randomisation balances known and unknown prognostic factors between arms only at the moment of allocation; the instant you remove people who dropped out, you are comparing a selected subgroup and the balance is gone, because the reasons people leave trials (side effects, lack of benefit, worsening illness) are related to outcome.

Here 80 were allocated to each arm. The 17 probiotic and 11 sertraline participants who did not complete still belong to their original arms, so the response rate in each arm is calculated out of 80. Those with missing outcomes are handled by a pre-specified rule for missing data, often treating them as non-responders in the primary analysis.

The exam offers subtracted denominators (63, 69) as tempting options. Whenever a stem reports who dropped out, the trap is to subtract them; the intention-to-treat answer is the original randomised numbers.

Rule: Analyse as randomised: every participant stays in the arm they were allocated to, whatever happened next.
Trap: Subtracting the drop-outs from each arm, which produces a per-protocol analysis.
The denominator stays at 80 in each arm: the 17 and 11 who dropped out remain in the crowd they were randomised to, so response is reported out of 80, not 63 or 69.

Source: Hollis S, Campbell F (1999). What is meant by intention to treat analysis? Survey of published randomised controlled trials. BMJ, 319: 670-674.

Challenge 17 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.22

Participant flow and reported denominators in a trial of supervised exercise for adolescent depression
In a trial of supervised exercise versus a waiting list for adolescents with depression, 120 participants were randomised equally to the two arms. Nine in the exercise arm never attended a session and 14 in the waiting-list arm withdrew before the final visit. The authors report remission out of 60 in each arm, counting every randomised participant. The table shows the flow and the denominators. Which analytical approach have they used?
  1. Per-protocol analysis
  2. Intention-to-treat analysis
  3. As-treated analysis
  4. Complete-case analysis
  5. Stratified analysis
Show the working
Answer: B Intention-to-treat analysis

There are several ways to decide who goes into which group at analysis. Intention to treat keeps the randomised groups intact. Per-protocol keeps only those who followed the protocol. As-treated regroups people by the treatment they actually received. Complete-case keeps only those with a measured outcome. Only the first preserves the balance that randomisation created.

The authors here used 60 and 60, the numbers randomised, and counted the nine non-attenders and 14 withdrawals in their original arms. That is intention to treat. It gives a conservative estimate of the effect of offering the treatment in practice, because non-adherers dilute the apparent benefit, and that is exactly the pragmatic question most trials want to answer.

The exam phrases this as 'reported out of all randomised' or 'regardless of compliance'. Either phrase is a direct cue for intention to treat.

Rule: Analysed as randomised, with all participants and no re-grouping, is intention to treat.
Trap: Confusing intention to treat with as-treated analysis, which sounds similar but regroups participants by what they actually received.

The table shows the results of a three-arm pragmatic trial in Ireland that compared home-based treatment (n = 60), a day hospital programme (n = 60) and standard community mental health team care (n = 60) for young people with a first episode of psychosis, with follow-up at 18 months. Non-completion of the allocated treatment was 15 in the home-based arm, 24 in the day hospital arm and 12 in the standard care arm. On a predefined categorical outcome, 25% in the home-based arm, 20% in the day hospital arm and 22% in standard care showed a satisfactory clinical response. Although non-completion was highest in the day hospital arm, every participant was analysed in the arm to which they were originally allocated. This approach is best described as
  1. Per-protocol analysis
  2. Intention to treat analysis
  3. Last observation carried forward
  4. Sensitivity analysis

Show the working
Answer: B Intention to treat analysis

Differential dropout is the central threat that intention to treat guards against. If more people leave one arm than another, the completers in that arm are a selected subgroup, and comparing completers across arms would compare different sorts of people, not different treatments.

Here the day hospital arm lost 24 of 60 participants but all 60 were kept in the day hospital group for analysis. This keeps the randomised balance and gives an estimate of the effect of offering day hospital care in practice.

Exam stems describe the strategy in words (analysed according to original assignment) and ask you to name it; the answer is always intention to treat.

Rule: Analysis by original allocation, regardless of what was received, is intention to treat.
Trap: Confusing a missing-data technique such as LOCF with the intention to treat principle.

Challenge 19 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23
Meta-analysis of nine randomised trialsResult
OutcomeRemission
Pooled odds ratio, augmentation versus placebo3.1
95% confidence interval1.9 to 5.0
HeterogeneityNo evidence
Pooled result of nine trials of second-generation antipsychotic augmentation in treatment-resistant depression
The table shows the pooled result of a meta-analysis of nine randomised trials of augmentation with a second-generation antipsychotic in treatment-resistant depression. Which conclusion is justified?
  1. Patients receiving augmentation are 3.1 times as likely to remit as those receiving placebo
  2. A new trial of the same comparison would be expected to produce an odds ratio between 1.9 and 5.0
  3. Publication bias can be ruled out
  4. The pooled treatment effect is statistically significant
  5. The absence of heterogeneity shows that the included trials were free of bias
Show the working
Answer: D The pooled treatment effect is statistically significant

For a ratio measure the null value is 1. If the 95% confidence interval excludes 1, the corresponding two-sided test would give p < 0.05, so the effect is statistically significant. The interval also conveys precision and the plausible range of the true pooled effect. It does not describe where any single future trial would land, which would be a prediction interval and would be wider.

Here the interval is 1.9 to 5.0, entirely above 1, so remission is significantly more likely with augmentation. The odds ratio of 3.1 cannot be read as 'three times as likely', because odds and probabilities diverge when the outcome is common, and remission in these trials is not rare. The lack of heterogeneity tells you the trials agree with each other, not that unpublished negative trials do not exist.

The exam surrounds the one plain statistical fact (interval excludes 1, therefore significant) with over-interpretations: odds read as risks, a confidence interval read as a prediction interval, and homogeneity read as proof of freedom from bias or publication bias. Check each statement against its definition; usually only the plain fact survives.

Rule: A 95% CI for an odds ratio that excludes 1 means the pooled effect is statistically significant, and that is all it means.
Trap: Reading the confidence interval as the range of results a new trial would show.
The whole interval from 1.9 to 5.0 sits above the null value of 1, which is all that is needed to call the pooled effect statistically significant

Source: Gardner MJ, Altman DG (1986). Confidence intervals rather than P values: estimation rather than hypothesis testing. BMJ, 292: 746-750.

Challenge 20 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23
Standardised mean difference in symptom improvement, new antipsychotic versus comparator antipsychotic, ten trials
The forest plot summarises ten randomised trials comparing a new antipsychotic with an established comparator in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. The outcome is the standardised mean difference in symptom improvement; positive values favour the new drug and negative values favour the comparator. How many of the trials show the new drug to be statistically significantly better than the comparator?
  1. 4
  2. 5
  3. 6
  4. 7
  5. 8
Show the working
Answer: C 6

Each horizontal line on a forest plot is a 95% confidence interval for one trial. If the line touches or crosses the vertical null line, that trial on its own could not reject the null hypothesis at the 5% level. If the line lies wholly to one side, the trial is significant in that direction. For a standardised mean difference the null is zero.

Going down the plot: Adeyemi (0.35 to 0.85), Brenner (0.02 to 0.58), Castillo (0.05 to 0.65), Dubois (0.10 to 1.70), Farah (0.15 to 0.75) and Grant (0.13 to 0.37) all sit entirely to the right of zero: six trials. Eriksen, Hoffmann, Ibrahim and Jansen cross zero and are not individually significant, even though Hoffmann's point estimate is large.

The exam expects you to count intervals, not point estimates. Two of the significant trials here only just clear zero, which is where candidates lose the count; check each lower limit explicitly.

Rule: On a forest plot a trial is significant when its whole confidence interval sits on one side of the null line (0 for differences, 1 for ratios).
Trap: Counting trials whose point estimate favours the drug rather than those whose whole interval does.

Challenge 21 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23
Standardised mean difference in symptom improvement, new antipsychotic versus comparator antipsychotic, ten trials
The forest plot summarises ten randomised trials comparing a new antipsychotic with an established comparator in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. The outcome is the standardised mean difference in symptom improvement; positive values favour the new drug and negative values favour the comparator. Which of the following conclusions from the plot is most correct?
  1. The effect size in Castillo 2011 was larger than in Dubois 2012
  2. The confidence interval for Grant 2015 is extremely wide
  3. The effect size in Hoffmann 2016 was larger than in Grant 2015, although Hoffmann was not statistically significant
  4. Because the interval for Jansen 2018 crosses zero, that trial shows the drug has no clinical effect
  5. The heterogeneity statistics show statistically significant heterogeneity
Show the working
Answer: C The effect size in Hoffmann 2016 was larger than in Grant 2015, although Hoffmann was not statistically significant

A forest plot carries three separate pieces of information for each trial: where the square sits (the effect size), how long the line is (precision, driven by sample size) and whether the line crosses the null (significance). A trial can have a large effect yet be non-significant if it is small and imprecise, and a trial with a modest effect can be highly significant if it is large.

Hoffmann 2016 is the imprecise-but-large example: estimate 0.60, interval minus 0.05 to 1.25, weight 1.6%. Grant 2015 is the opposite: estimate 0.25, interval 0.13 to 0.37, weight 46.9%. So Hoffmann's effect size is larger even though only Grant is significant. The other options each confuse two of the three ideas, or misread the heterogeneity p value of 0.07 as significant.

The exam's favourite distractor is 'crosses the line, therefore clinically insignificant'. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; the interval tells you the data are compatible with anything from a tiny harm to a large benefit.

Rule: Point estimate = size of effect; interval width = precision; crossing the null = not significant. Keep the three ideas separate.
Trap: Equating a confidence interval that crosses the null with proof of no effect.

Challenge 22 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23
Standardised mean difference in symptom improvement, new antipsychotic versus comparator antipsychotic, ten trials
The forest plot summarises ten randomised trials comparing a new antipsychotic with an established comparator in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. The outcome is the standardised mean difference in symptom improvement; positive values favour the new drug and negative values favour the comparator. What is the overall conclusion from the pooled result?
  1. The new drug is much more effective than the comparator
  2. The new drug is modestly more effective than the comparator
  3. There is no clinically meaningful difference between the two drugs
  4. There is no statistically significant difference between the two drugs
  5. The new drug is significantly less effective than the comparator
Show the working
Answer: B The new drug is modestly more effective than the comparator

The diamond at the bottom of a forest plot is the pooled estimate; its centre is the point estimate and its width is the 95% confidence interval. For standardised mean differences the usual descriptive bands are about 0.2 small, 0.5 moderate and 0.8 large, although what counts as clinically meaningful depends on the condition and the alternatives.

Here the pooled standardised mean difference is 0.30 (0.22 to 0.38). The interval excludes zero with a large z, so the advantage is clearly real, but the size is small to moderate: patients on the new drug improve by about a third of a standard deviation more than those on the comparator. In treatment-resistant illness that is a worthwhile gain, not a transformation.

The exam phrases the choice as 'much more', 'slightly more' and 'no difference'. Match the pooled point estimate to the effect size bands, then confirm significance from the interval.

Rule: Read the diamond: its position gives the size of the pooled effect and whether it touches the null line gives significance.
Trap: Confusing statistical significance (clearly present) with a large effect (absent).

Challenge 23 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23
Standardised mean difference in symptom improvement, new antipsychotic versus comparator antipsychotic, ten trials
The forest plot summarises ten randomised trials comparing a new antipsychotic with an established comparator in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. The outcome is the standardised mean difference in symptom improvement; positive values favour the new drug and negative values favour the comparator. Which trial produced the most precise estimate?
  1. Adeyemi 2009
  2. Dubois 2012
  3. Grant 2015
  4. Ibrahim 2017
  5. Jansen 2018
Show the working
Answer: C Grant 2015

Precision describes how tightly the data pin down the estimate, and on a forest plot it appears in three equivalent ways: the shortest horizontal line, the largest square (because inverse-variance weights are proportional to 1/SE squared) and the biggest percentage weight. Precision reflects sample size and outcome variability, not the direction or size of the effect.

Grant 2015 has the shortest line, spanning only 0.24 units, and carries 46.9% of the weight, so it is the most precise trial and pulls the pooled estimate strongly towards its own value of 0.25. Dubois 2012, with the biggest point estimate, is the least precise (weight 1.0%) and barely influences the pooled result.

The exam separates 'most precise' from 'most significant' and 'largest effect'. Precision is purely about interval width; it says nothing about which side of the null the interval sits.

Rule: Precision = narrow confidence interval = big square = large weight; it is independent of where the estimate sits.
Trap: Choosing the trial with the largest effect or the most impressive significance instead of the narrowest interval.

Challenge 24 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23
Relapse at 12 months: structured relapse-prevention programme versus usual care in eight randomised trials (events/total shown for each arm)
A systematic review pooled eight randomised trials of a structured relapse-prevention programme versus usual care in people with recurrent depression, with relapse within 12 months as the outcome. The forest plot shows the risk ratio for relapse with events and totals for each arm. Which study has the least influence on the pooled estimate?
  1. Achebe 2004
  2. Doyle 2011
  3. Fernandes 2014
  4. Gallagher 2016
  5. Esposito 2012
Show the working
Answer: C Fernandes 2014

In a meta-analysis each study is weighted, usually by the inverse of its variance, so that precise studies count for more. The weight column and the square size on the forest plot show this directly. The pooled estimate is the weighted average of the study estimates, so the smallest weight means the smallest contribution.

Reading the weight column: Esposito 31.2%, Gallagher 22.3%, Bergstrom 20.5%, Achebe 8.6%, Chandra 7.2%, Hussain 7.1%, Doyle 2.3% and Fernandes 0.8%. Fernandes 2014 is the least influential by a clear margin, which matches its tiny square and its very long confidence line.

The exam may tempt you towards a study with a dramatic point estimate (Fernandes has the largest apparent effect, RR 0.25) or one far from the others. Influence is about weight, not about how striking the estimate looks.

Rule: The study with the smallest weight (smallest square) has the least influence on the pooled estimate.
Trap: Confusing a large or unusual point estimate with large influence.

Challenge 25 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23
Relapse at 12 months: structured relapse-prevention programme versus usual care in eight randomised trials (events/total shown for each arm)
A systematic review pooled eight randomised trials of a structured relapse-prevention programme versus usual care in people with recurrent depression, with relapse within 12 months as the outcome. The forest plot shows the risk ratio for relapse with events and totals for each arm. One study is drawn with an arrowhead at the end of its horizontal line. What does the arrowhead indicate?
  1. Its point estimate was larger than those of the other trials
  2. Its confidence interval extends beyond the plotted axis, so its estimate is very imprecise
  3. Its sample was more representative of the target population
  4. It had the longest follow-up of the included trials
  5. It was the largest trial in the review
Show the working
Answer: B Its confidence interval extends beyond the plotted axis, so its estimate is very imprecise

The horizontal line for each study is its 95% confidence interval. Its length is a direct visual measure of imprecision, which comes mainly from small numbers of participants and events. When an interval is so wide that it would run past the edge of the plotted scale, software truncates the line and adds an arrowhead to say 'this continues'.

Here Fernandes 2014 randomised 8 people per arm and saw 1 and 4 events. Its risk ratio of 0.25 has a confidence interval from 0.04 to 1.77. The axis runs from 0.1 to 10, so the lower limit lies off the plot and the line is arrowed. Compare Esposito 2012, with 320 participants, whose interval 0.55 to 1.01 fits comfortably.

The exam pairs the arrow with distractors about sample size and effect size. Remember that long lines mean small, imprecise studies, and arrows are just long lines that did not fit.

Rule: An arrowhead on a forest plot means the confidence interval runs off the axis: a very imprecise study.
Trap: Reading the arrow as a sign of a large or important trial.
A risk ratio of 0.25 built from 1 relapse versus 4 in 8 people a side: a single event either way would change it enormously, which is why the interval stretches from 0.04 to 1.77 and runs off the axis.

Source: Petrie A, Sabin C (2019). Medical Statistics at a Glance, 4th ed. Wiley Blackwell.

Challenge 26 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23
Relapse at 12 months: structured relapse-prevention programme versus usual care in eight randomised trials (events/total shown for each arm)
A systematic review pooled eight randomised trials of a structured relapse-prevention programme versus usual care in people with recurrent depression, with relapse within 12 months as the outcome. The forest plot shows the risk ratio for relapse with events and totals for each arm. Which individual study shows a statistically significant benefit of the programme on its own?
  1. Esposito 2012
  2. Chandra 2009
  3. Fernandes 2014
  4. Bergstrom 2007
  5. Gallagher 2016
Show the working
Answer: B Chandra 2009

For a ratio measure the line of no effect is 1. A study's 95% confidence interval that lies wholly to one side of 1 corresponds to p < 0.05 for that study; an interval that touches or crosses 1 does not. On a forest plot this is read by checking whether the study's horizontal line crosses the vertical line.

Checking each: Achebe 0.37 to 1.20 crosses; Bergstrom 0.54 to 1.15 crosses; Chandra 0.26 to 0.95 does not; Doyle 0.16 to 1.55 crosses; Esposito 0.55 to 1.01 just crosses; Fernandes 0.04 to 1.77 crosses; Gallagher 0.66 to 1.37 crosses; Hussain 0.36 to 1.32 crosses. Only Chandra 2009 is significant on its own, although the pooled estimate, 0.63 to 0.89, clearly is.

Two traps are built in: the big trial whose upper limit sits at 1.01, and the small trial with the dramatic point estimate. Both fail the test. Note also that most trials being individually non-significant while the pooled result is significant is precisely why meta-analysis exists.

Rule: A study is significant on its own only if its confidence interval excludes the line of no effect.
Trap: Picking the largest point estimate or the largest trial instead of checking the interval against 1.
StudyRR95% CIIncludes 1?Significant alone?
Achebe 20040.670.37 to 1.20YesNo
Bergstrom 20070.790.54 to 1.15YesNo
Chandra 20090.500.26 to 0.95NoYes
Doyle 20110.500.16 to 1.55YesNo
Esposito 20120.750.55 to 1.01YesNo
Fernandes 20140.250.04 to 1.77YesNo
Gallagher 20160.950.66 to 1.37YesNo
Hussain 20180.690.36 to 1.32YesNo
Pooled0.750.63 to 0.89NoYes
Interval by interval: only Chandra 2009 (0.26 to 0.95) lies wholly below 1; Esposito's upper limit of 1.01 just includes it.

Source: Gardner MJ, Altman DG (1986). Confidence intervals rather than P values: estimation rather than hypothesis testing. BMJ, 292: 746-750.

Challenge 27 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23
Remission of insomnia at 12 weeks: digital sleep programme versus waiting list in five randomised trials
The forest plot summarises five trials of a digital sleep programme for insomnia. Which feature of the plot shows the weight given to each study in the meta-analysis?
  1. The length of the horizontal line for the study
  2. The size of the square marking the study's estimate
  3. The study's position in the list
  4. The distance of the square from the line of no effect
  5. Weight cannot be judged from the plot
Show the working
Answer: B The size of the square marking the study's estimate

Each study's square on a forest plot has an area proportional to its weight in the pooled analysis. Weight is usually the inverse of the variance of the study's estimate, so large, precise studies get big squares and narrow intervals, and small studies get tiny squares and long lines. The square is enlarged on purpose so that the eye is drawn to the studies that matter most and away from small outliers whose point estimates may look dramatic.

In this plot Duarte 2016 and Byrne 2012 carry 39.9% and 30.7% of the weight and have the largest squares; Ahmed, Clarke and Eneh carry between 7% and 13% each and have small squares with long lines. The pooled diamond at 1.76 sits close to the two big squares, as it should.

The exam's favourite wrong answer is the line length. Remember the division of labour: square for weight, line for precision, position along the axis for effect size, diamond for the pooled estimate.

Rule: On a forest plot, square size = study weight.
Trap: Choosing the line length because precision and weight are related.
StudyWeight (%)Square95% CILine length

Byrne 201230.71.45 to 3.041.59
Clarke 20149.80.70 to 2.601.90
Duarte 201639.9Largest1.30 to 2.491.19
Eneh 20196.9Smallest0.55 to 2.622.07

Square area tracks the weight column: Duarte 39.9% is the biggest square and Eneh 6.9% the smallest, while line length (2.07 for Eneh, 1.19 for Duarte) runs the other way.

Source: Petrie A, Sabin C (2019). Medical Statistics at a Glance, 4th ed. Wiley Blackwell.

Challenge 28 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23
Standardised mean difference in end-point depression score, SNRI versus SSRI, grouped by SNRI (negative values favour the SNRI)
The figure comes from a review comparing serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors with SSRIs for major depression, with the end-point depression score as the outcome and trials grouped by the SNRI studied. Negative values favour the SNRI. What is this type of graph called?
  1. Galbraith plot
  2. Funnel plot
  3. L'Abbe plot
  4. Forest plot
  5. Scatter plot
Show the working
Answer: D Forest plot

The forest plot is the standard display of a meta-analysis. Its anatomy is fixed: study labels down the left, a square for each point estimate sized by weight, a horizontal line for each confidence interval, a vertical line of no effect (here 0, because the measure is a standardised mean difference), and a diamond whose centre and width give the pooled estimate and its interval. Subgroups each get their own diamond, with an overall diamond at the bottom.

In the figure every one of those elements is present, including subtotal diamonds for each SNRI and heterogeneity statistics under each group. The informal name blobbogram refers to the 'blobs', the squares, that march down the plot.

The exam often tests the name first and then interrogates the content. Once you have identified the forest plot, the follow-up questions ask you to read weights, direction, significance and heterogeneity from it.

Rule: Study list, squares with horizontal intervals, line of no effect, diamond = forest plot (blobbogram).
Trap: Choosing Galbraith or funnel because the plot concerns a meta-analysis.
TermFormula or meaningThis item
Galbraith plotz against 1/SE with a regression lineNot this
Funnel plotEffect against precision, no study namesNot this
L'Abbe plotExperimental against control event rateNot this
Forest plotStudy list, squares with horizontal intervals, line of no effect, subgroup and overall diamondsYes: every element is present
Scatter plotPaired observationsNot this
The six labelled studies, three subtotal diamonds and one overall diamond make this a forest plot (blobbogram).

Source: Petrie A, Sabin C (2019). Medical Statistics at a Glance, 4th ed. Wiley Blackwell.

Challenge 29 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23
Standardised mean difference in end-point depression score, SNRI versus SSRI, grouped by SNRI (negative values favour the SNRI)
The figure comes from a review comparing serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors with SSRIs for major depression, with the end-point depression score as the outcome and trials grouped by the SNRI studied. Negative values favour the SNRI. Which study's result favours the SSRI rather than the SNRI?
  1. Anand 2008
  2. Baxter 2010
  3. Dorn 2011
  4. Ekwueme 2014
  5. Fournier 2016
Show the working
Answer: D Ekwueme 2014

The two labels beneath a forest plot tell you which side means what. Here negative differences favour the SNRI and positive differences favour the SSRI. A study 'favours' whichever side its square sits on, regardless of whether its interval crosses the line; crossing tells you about significance, not direction.

Only Ekwueme 2014 has a positive point estimate (+0.05) and so sits to the right of zero on the SSRI side. Its interval runs from -0.30 to 0.40, so the result is compatible with either drug being slightly better, but the point estimate favours the SSRI. All the other five studies sit to the left.

The exam may invert the labels in another plot so that the right-hand side favours the intervention. Never assume left means better; read the labels every time.

Rule: Read direction from the side of the line of no effect the point estimate falls on, using the axis labels.
Trap: Assuming the left of the plot always favours the treatment of interest.

Baxter 2010-0.18-0.40 to 0.04Left: favours SNRIYes
Costa 2012-0.12-0.44 to 0.20Left: favours SNRIYes
Dorn 2011-0.25-0.47 to -0.03Left: favours SNRINo
Ekwueme 2014+0.05-0.30 to 0.40Right: favours SSRIYes
Fournier 2016-0.22-0.52 to 0.08Left: favours SNRIYes
Direction is the sign of the point estimate: only Ekwueme 2014 (+0.05) sits on the SSRI side, though its interval (-0.30 to 0.40) also crosses zero.

Challenge 30 · 13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23
Standardised mean difference in end-point depression score, SNRI versus SSRI, grouped by SNRI (negative values favour the SNRI)
The figure comes from a review comparing serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors with SSRIs for major depression, with the end-point depression score as the outcome and trials grouped by the SNRI studied. Negative values favour the SNRI. Which result is the most precise?
  1. Baxter 2010
  2. Dorn 2011
  3. The venlafaxine subgroup estimate
  4. The overall pooled estimate
  5. Fournier 2016
Show the working
Answer: D The overall pooled estimate

Precision is the inverse of variance, and on a forest plot it is seen as the width of the confidence interval: shorter line, more precise. Pooling adds information, so a subgroup estimate is more precise than any of its trials and the overall estimate, drawing on every trial, is normally the most precise result on the plot. That gain in precision is one of the two main reasons for meta-analysis.

Measuring the widths: Baxter and Dorn 0.44; Anand 0.50; Fournier 0.60; Costa 0.64; Ekwueme 0.70; venlafaxine subtotal 0.30; duloxetine subtotal 0.37; milnacipran subtotal 0.60 (it is just Fournier); overall 0.21. The overall estimate wins.

The exam sometimes offers two pooled results, a subgroup and the overall, and asks you to compare their widths by eye. Do the subtraction rather than trusting the look of the diamonds.

Rule: Precision = narrowness of the confidence interval; pooling more studies gives the narrowest interval.
Trap: Choosing the largest single trial rather than a pooled estimate.
Result95% CIWidthRank
Overall pooled estimate-0.30 to -0.090.211 (most precise)
Venlafaxine subgroup-0.36 to -0.060.302
Duloxetine subgroup-0.35 to 0.020.373
Baxter 2010-0.40 to 0.040.444 (equal)
Dorn 2011-0.47 to -0.030.444 (equal)
Fournier 2016-0.52 to 0.080.60widest of the options
Interval widths by subtraction: the overall estimate at 0.21 is narrower than any subgroup or single trial.

Source: Gardner MJ, Altman DG (1986). Confidence intervals rather than P values: estimation rather than hypothesis testing. BMJ, 292: 746-750.

CARD 1
Effect size (Cohen's d) for processing speed in unaffected first-degree relatives of people with bipolar disorder versus healthy controls, by methodological tier
13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23

A meta-analytic review examined processing speed in unaffected first-degree relatives of people with bipolar disorder compared with healthy controls. Studies were grouped into three methodological tiers: Tier 1 used a structured diagnostic interview and a…

Which statistical measure was used to produce the figure?
C) Cohen's d

Remember. Two groups, continuous outcome, unit-free effect size = Cohen's d (the standardised mean difference). (Effect size between two groups = Cohen's d)

Trap. Choosing Cohen's kappa because the name Cohen appears.

Why not the others.
A) Cohen's kappa: Cohen's kappa measures agreement between raters beyond chance; it is not a between-group effect size.
B) Pearson's r: Pearson's r is a correlation between two continuous variables in the same people.

Relapse at 12 months: family intervention versus treatment as usual, 7 randomised trials (events/total shown for family intervention then treatment as usual)
13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.23

The forest plot summarises seven randomised trials of family intervention versus treatment as usual in schizophrenia, with relapse at 12 months as the outcome, reported as odds ratios. The horizontal axis runs from 0. 05 to 5 and its tick marks are spaced…

Why is a logarithmic axis used for a forest plot of odds ratios?
B) So that ratios of the same size in either direction, such as 0.5 and 2, sit at equal distances from the line of no effect and each confidence interval appears symmetrical about its point estimate

Remember. Ratio measures (OR, RR, HR) are analysed and plotted on the log scale: 0.5 and 2 are mirror images about 1. (Ratios live on a log axis: 0.5 and 2 are the same distance from 1)

Trap. Reading equal distances on a log axis as equal differences in odds ratio.

Why not the others.
A) Because odds ratios cannot be negative, so a linear axis cannot be drawn: A linear axis can be drawn for odds ratios; it is simply misleading, because it squashes everything below 1 into a narrow strip.
C) To make small trials look more precise than they are: Precision is shown by the length of the line and the size of the square, which the log scale does not inflate.

B) Family intervention was associated with fewer relapses than treatment as usual in that trial

Trap. Assuming a bigger symbol means a bigger effect.

Why not the others.

C) One trial included in the meta-analysis

What is this graph called?
C) L'Abbe plot

Remember. Event rate in the treated arm against event rate in the control arm = L'Abbe plot. (Two event rates with a diagonal = L'Abbe)

Trap. Mistaking any plot with a diagonal line for a Bland-Altman plot or a scatter of individuals.

A) Funnel plot: A funnel plot shows effect size against precision or study size and is used to look for publication bias.

CARD 17
Relapse at 12 months: family intervention versus treatment as usual, 7 randomised trials (events/total shown for family intervention then treatment as usual)
13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.25

The forest plot summarises seven randomised trials of family intervention versus treatment as usual in schizophrenia, with relapse at 12 months as the outcome, reported as odds ratios. The heterogeneity line reports I2 = 31%.

Which is the best interpretation?
B) About 31% of the variability in effect estimates across trials is due to genuine differences between studies rather than chance, which is low to moderate heterogeneity

Remember. I2 = percentage of between-study variation due to heterogeneity; 25% low, 50% moderate, 75% high. (I2 = (Q minus df) / Q, the share of spread that is real)

Trap. Reading I2 as a p value or as a fraction of studies.

Why not the others.
A) 31% of the trials gave results that disagree with the pooled estimate: I2 is not a count or proportion of trials.
C) There is a 31% probability that the pooled result is due to chance: The probability of chance is addressed by the p value for the overall effect (p < 0.00001), not by I2.

The funnel plot shows 12 placebo-controlled trials of lithium augmentation in treatment-resistant depression, plotting each trial's odds ratio for response against its standard error, with the pooled estimate as a vertical line and pseudo 95% limits…

What does this pattern most strongly suggest?
B) Publication bias, with small trials showing no benefit or harm missing from the literature

Remember. An empty lower corner of the funnel on the 'no effect' side suggests publication bias. (Lopsided funnel, empty lower corner = suspect publication bias)

Trap. Concluding that the treatment does not work, rather than that its benefit may be overstated.

Why not the others.
A) The large trials are biased: Large trials near the pooled line are what you expect; it is the small trials that are skewed.
C) Lithium augmentation is ineffective: Every trial, large and small, lies to the right of 1 (log OR above 0), so the evidence favours benefit; the question is whether its size is exaggerated.

13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.25

The funnel plot shows 12 placebo-controlled trials of lithium augmentation in treatment-resistant depression, plotting each trial's odds ratio for response against its standard error, with the pooled estimate as a vertical line and pseudo 95% limits…

Which trials are plotted nearest the top of the funnel?
C) Those with the smallest standard errors, generally the largest trials

Remember. Funnel plot: x = effect, y = precision (SE, with 0 at the top). (Top of the funnel = most precise = biggest trials)

Trap. Reading the vertical axis as effect size or as sample size in the wrong direction.

Why not the others.
A) Those with the largest odds ratios: Effect size is on the horizontal axis, not the vertical.
B) Those published most recently: Year of publication is not an axis of a funnel plot.

Funnel plot of 12 placebo-controlled trials of lithium augmentation for treatment-resistant depression (response at 6 weeks)
13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.25

The funnel plot shows 12 placebo-controlled trials of lithium augmentation in treatment-resistant depression, plotting each trial's odds ratio for response against its standard error, with the pooled estimate as a vertical line and pseudo 95% limits…

If the asymmetry is due to publication bias, what is the most likely consequence for the meta-analysis?
  1. The pooled odds ratio underestimates the true benefit of lithium augmentation
  2. The pooled odds ratio overestimates the true benefit of lithium augmentation
  3. The pooled confidence interval is too narrow but the estimate is unbiased
  4. The I2 statistic will be zero
  5. The random-effects estimate will be less affected than the fixed-effect estimate
B) The pooled odds ratio overestimates the true benefit of lithium augmentation

Remember. Publication bias usually exaggerates the pooled effect in favour of the intervention. (Missing null trials = pooled effect looks better than it is)

Trap. Thinking bias widens the interval rather than shifting the estimate.

Why not the others.
A) The pooled odds ratio underestimates the true benefit of lithium augmentation: Missing studies lie on the 'no benefit' side, so their absence inflates, not deflates, the apparent effect.
C) The pooled confidence interval is too narrow but the estimate is unbiased: The estimate itself is biased when a systematic set of results is missing; this is not merely a precision problem.

13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.25

A reviewer collecting trials of a herbal extract for generalised anxiety disorder notices that small trials tend to appear in print only when they favour the extract, whereas larger trials are published whatever they show. The funnel plot of the included…

What does the plot demonstrate?
C) Asymmetry caused by the absence of small trials with null or unfavourable results

Remember. Publication bias shows as funnel plot asymmetry: a gap where small, null or negative studies should be. (Empty lower corner of the funnel = missing small negative studies)

Trap. Attributing the asymmetry to the large studies rather than to the missing small ones.

Why not the others.
A) A symmetrical funnel, as expected when all trials are published: The plot is visibly lopsided: the lower right is populated and the lower left is empty.
B) Asymmetry caused by the presence of large trials with results in both directions: Large trials sit at the top of the funnel near the pooled estimate; they are not the cause of the asymmetry.

13.8 Intention to treat, missing data and meta-analysis · 3.2.25

At a journal club a trainee presents the funnel plot shown, drawn from a systematic review of a mindfulness app for stress in healthcare staff, and argues that it shows publication bias.

Which of the following is the most likely mechanism behind publication bias of this kind?
  1. Journal editors accept only papers written by recognised experts
  2. Systematic reviewers discard weaker studies before pooling
  3. Investigators do not submit studies with null or negative results for publication
  4. Authors send small studies to journals that are not indexed in major databases
  5. Editors accept only papers whose conclusions they agree with
C) Investigators do not submit studies with null or negative results for publication

Remember. Publication bias arises mostly because null and negative studies are never submitted, not because journals reject them. (File drawer: negative studies are not submitted)

Trap. Blaming editors rather than non-submission by investigators.

Why not the others.
A) Journal editors accept only papers written by recognised experts: Author seniority is not the dominant driver of what reaches print.
B) Systematic reviewers discard weaker studies before pooling: Reviewers' selection decisions are part of the review method, not of publication bias.
